newsitem.title: UK: European coffee body tells growers to revoke curbs.
newsitem.headline: European coffee body tells growers to revoke curbs.

text.p: The European coffee trade has told coffee producers to revoke their "unilateral" supply curbs or face the longer-term risk of a boom and bust cycle which it said could harm both growers and consumers.

The European Coffee Federation (ECF), which groups the region's roasters and traders, also warned of sliding coffee consumption across Europe due to retail price hikes following the surge in world green coffee prices.

In a statement issued on Wednesday after the ECF annual meeting in Vienna on Tuesday, the group said "in the longer term there is a risk of a boom-bust cycle' with alternating periods of very high and very low prices".
"The ECF is convinced that such 'boom-bust cycles' are harmful for producing countries as well as for the coffee sector in consuming countries," it said.
It said the current price level would encourage over-production, resulting in an over-supply situation in two or three years' time and substantially lower prices.

"We therefore call on the coffee producing countries to act responsibly in their production and export activities, in the common interest of a sound long term development of the world coffee market, and to revoke unilateral export limitations," it said.
The 14-member Association of Coffee Producing Countries (ACPC) led by Brazil agreed on March 21 to extend their cartel-style export quotas for 12 more months.
The deal was cut against a backdrop of a rally that has taken benchmark for green, unroasted beans upwards by 80 to 100 percent since January.
New York futures for arabica type of beans, the high quality coffee, hit a 20-year high of $3.18 per pound on May 29. It has fallen back to trade around $2.58 on Wednesday.

The rally on the back of low stocks and tight Latin American supplies has forced roasters to put up their retail prices, a trend the ECF said could endanger the level of consumption throughout Europe.
Consumers will try to compensate for the higher shop prices buy buying lower quality coffee or switch to cheaper hot beverages such as tea.
"The ECF is concerned that it will be difficult to recapture lost ground quickly," the statement added.
"...The shift to lower quality coffees will be detrimental since drinking good quality coffee is the best stimulus for increasing consumption," it said.
